13.14.0.en: only I will justify my way before him [15].

13.14.1.en: Job resolved to hold fast to his way, and was never willing to give up the rest he had found in walking uprightly with God, however great his afflictions, even to death. So he says with Hezekiah: "Remember now, O LORD, how I have walked before thee in truth and with a perfect heart" (2 Kgs 20:3). Even if trials drive me to my death, I remain trusting in Him, or full of hope in Him, that I may be vindicated before Him. I am His friend and He is my friend; I will not give up clinging to Him, even if He appears as an enemy to me who delivers me to trials unto death.

13.14.2.en: * [Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him] [15]... A man is truly patient when calamities befall him... Here the righteous mind is distinguished from the wicked; for in the midst of affliction, the former knows that the glory of Almighty God is not shaken by worldly events, and so does not collapse with the collapse of outward glory, but rather affirms that it is stronger when it loses temporal goods.

13.14.4.en: * "For as the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so our consolation also aboundeth by Christ" (2 Cor 1:5)... He lifts up our souls by counting these sufferings as His own; what joy fills us to be partakers with Christ, for whose sake we suffer! By faith we perceive the new birth and the resurrection. Those who truly believe in the risen Jesus must offer themselves to sufferings. And those who share in His sufferings will also rise with Him. "That I may know him, and the power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings, being made conformable unto his death; if by any means I might attain unto the resurrection of the dead" (Phil 3:10-11).

13.14.5.en: * The loving man who clings to God always is not harmed by waves, however many; on the contrary, he comes out of them with new strength. But the weak, slack man falls often, even when there is nothing to trouble him.

13.14.6.en: St. John Chrysostom * If as the sufferings of Christ abound, so also the consolation by Christ increases, let us welcome the encouraging sufferings of Christ. Let them overflow in us, if we truly seek the overflowing consolation with which all who mourn are comforted, even if it is not alike for everyone. For if the consolation were alike for everyone, it would not have been written that as the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so our consolation by Christ abounds exceedingly. Those who share in the sufferings will also share in the consolation, according to their fellowship in the sufferings of Christ.

13.15.0.en: Origen He also shall be my salvation: for an hypocrite (a hypocrite) shall not come before him [16].

13.15.1.en: He does not mean here temporal salvation, for his hope of deliverance from his trials in this world and of returning to what he had been was almost nonexistent; rather he hopes for his eternal salvation, where he will meet with God and see Him face to face. As for the secret of his confidence in his eternal salvation, it is that he knows that his relationship with God has in it no hypocrisy or deviation, for God does not cling to hypocrites, and will not allow them to stand before Him enjoying His glory.

13.15.2.en: * [For a hypocrite shall not come before him] [16]... We must keep in mind that we come before the Lord in two ways.

13.15.3.en: We call ourselves to account for our sins here, and judge ourselves before Him and punish ourselves with weeping. For whenever we remember our awareness of the power of our Creator, we are like those who stand before Him. Thus Elijah, the man of God, rightly said: [As the LORD God of Israel liveth, before whom I stand] (a).

13.15.4.en: The other way is that we come before God when we present ourselves before His judgment seat only at the last judgment. So the hypocrite, in the final reckoning, comes before the Judge; but since he shuts his eyes against looking at his sins here and lamenting them, he refuses to come before the Lord... And since his mind is corrupted by the words of praise directed to him, he does not call it to recognize sin, nor does he realize that he opposes the inward Judge, and does not fear His firmness... Thus his eyes are not directed to the firmness of God, since he is greedy to please the eyes of men.

13.15.5.en: * [But I reprove my ways before him, he shall be my salvation] [15]. The Apostle Paul says: "For if we would judge ourselves, we should not be judged" (1 Cor 11:31). The Lord is our salvation insofar as we reprove our sins in the fear of God.

13.15.7.en: * I will judge myself, so that He may not judge me, who afterward will judge the living and the dead (2 Macc 7:18-19).

13.15.8.en: St. Augustine * [Consider yourself, then] until you attain the vision of God.

13.15.9.en: St. Basil the Great * Let this be your first concern, that you do not deceive yourself.

13.15.10.en: St. Melito, Bishop of Sardis * Hypocrisy is hateful to God and abhorred by men; it brings no reward, and is of no use at all for the salvation of the soul, but rather destroys it.

13.15.11.en: If anyone escapes by hypocrisy lest his affair be discovered, it is only for a while, for it does not last long, but everything is revealed, and brings shame upon its owner. Thus he is like an ugly woman whose outward adornment, put on her by artificial means, is stripped from her.

13.15.12.en: Hypocrisy is therefore foreign to the saints, for it is impossible that anything of what we do or say should escape the eyes of the Godhead, since it was said: [For there is nothing covered, that shall not be revealed; neither hid, that shall not be known] (Lk 12:2). If all our words and deeds will be revealed on the Day of Judgment, then hypocrisy is wearisome and without profit. It is fitting for us to be approved as true worshipers who serve God with sincere and open countenances.

13.16.0.en: St. Cyril the Great Hear diligently my speech, and my declaration with your ears [17].

13.16.1.en: He calls them again to cease their accusations and to give ear, so that they may enjoy with him the meeting with God through sincerity, purity and love.

13.16.2.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that Job repeats the word "hear" because he wants them not to hear only with their outward ears, but also to listen with their inward ears, so that they may understand the depths of his words in a spiritual way.

13.16.3.en: Behold now, I have ordered my cause;

13.17.0.en: I know that I shall be justified [18].

13.17.1.en: He has no need of their testimony, for he has ordered his cause well before God, and has presented to Him the sincerity of his conscience and the purity of his heart, and so enjoys innocence through the grace of God.

13.17.2.en: * [Behold, I am very near my judgment, I know that I shall be found righteous]. This is the judgment of which it is said in another book: [He shall bring forth thy righteousness as the light, and thy judgment as the noonday] (b). But he did not say: [I am already so], but [I am very near]. For if the judgment he means was not so as he experienced it, it will be so on the last day, when all are judged, and those who pray sincerely are found righteous: [Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors] (Mt 6:12). For through this forgiveness they are found righteous, since the sins they committed here are blotted out by the works of love they practiced (by their forgiveness of others).

13.17.3.en: St. Augustine * [Behold, I am near my Judge]. It is fitting for the adversary to have his tongue silenced, and for the Judge to be the one who speaks...

13.17.4.en: * [I know that I shall appear righteous], for I have fulfilled all the Law, and carried out all the commandments. I did not care about my unknown sins, and those I committed willingly, for I have washed them with prayer and tears. [I know that I shall appear righteous]. Although the enemy wishes to hide my righteousness by stirring up my companions to accuse me, even in this I shall appear righteous, when the veil of this present life is opened, while the clouds of the state of this life are corrupt; but even now I appear righteous as long as my patience stands to the end, and I shall show courage in trials to the very end.

13.17.5.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that what blessed Job said about himself carries humility, for God Himself testified of him that there is none like him on the earth, and there is a great difference between God's testimony to him and Job's saying about himself in his dispute with his friends, who had become his accusers that he was righteous. He refused to describe himself as greater than others, contenting himself with justifying himself against the accusations of his companions.

13.18.0.en: Who is he that will contend with me, that now I should hold my peace and give up the ghost? [19]

13.18.1.en: In assurance of God's wide mercies to sincere believers, he does not care about their contention, nor does he fear divine discipline, but in tranquility gives up his spirit and finds eternal rest.

13.18.2.en: Job presents to us a living picture of the Christian who enjoys a true vision of the work of the Cross in his life, how it freed him from the devil his adversary, and put him to shame, so that the enemy became under his feet. Thus he does not fear him nor tremble, but mocks him.

13.18.3.en: * Since he saw in his outward conduct no possibility for anyone to blame him, therefore in complete freedom he looks toward any accuser of his.

13.18.5.en: * The spirits fall into grief, and since they want our destruction, they are destroyed by us with the same destruction they desire for us. But their defeat does not mean that they leave us for good...

13.18.6.en: When their strength perishes and they fail in their struggle with us, we say: [Let them be ashamed and put to shame that seek after my soul to destroy it; let them be turned backward and put to shame that rejoice at my hurt] (Ps 40:14). And Jeremiah also says: "Let them be confounded that persecute me, but let not me be confounded: let them be dismayed, but let not me be dismayed: bring upon them the day of evil, and destroy them with double destruction" (Jer 17:18), since no one can doubt that when we have overcome them they perish with a double destruction.

13.18.7.en: Fr. Serenus * If you say that the opposing power is very strong, and that evil has complete dominion over man, then you ascribe injustice to God when He judges men for their submission to Satan, because Satan is very strong and subjects mankind with an irresistible force. In this way you make Satan greater and stronger than the soul, and then you tell me not to submit to Satan. This is like a fight between a young man and a small child, where the child, when defeated, is condemned for his defeat. This is a great injustice!

13.18.8.en: St. Macarius the Great * The thoughts of Satan are merely a mental image of something (or a deed) that is evil, and what enables it to take possession of us, or even simply to approach our mind, is the weakness of our faith. For after we have received the commandment, that we cast away from us all distractions and keep our hearts with all vigilance (Prov 4:23), and seek the Kingdom of God which is within us, when the mind has abandoned the heart and the aim we are pursuing, we have at once made room for Satan's imaginations, and the mind has become lax in accepting any evil counsel.

13.18.9.en: Even to this extent, Satan has no authority to move our thoughts; otherwise he would not have pity on us, but would plant in us all kinds of evil thoughts and allow us no good. Rather, his power is limited to merely offering false counsel at the beginning of every thought, to test to which side our heart inclines: does it incline to his counsel or to God's counsel? For they are opposites.

13.18.10.en: St. Mark the Ascetic * We go out from the house of our old father... since we were by nature children of wrath, even as others, fixing our eyes upon the things above.

13.19.s.en: 6. A cry to stop the discipline

13.19.0.en: 20 "Only do not two things unto me: then will I not hide myself from thee. 21 Withdraw thine hand far from me: and let not thy dread make me afraid. 22 Then call thou, and I will answer: or let me speak, and answer thou me."

13.19.1.en: Only do not two things unto me: then will I not hide myself from thee [20].

13.19.2.en: With all that has befallen Job, he does not want to hide from the face of God like his father Adam, but wants to appear in His presence.

13.19.3.en: Although Job confesses his sins in more than one place, he wants to be always with God. "Make me to know my transgression and my sin. Wherefore hidest thou thy face, and holdest me for thine enemy?" (Job 13:23-24).

13.19.4.en: Job desired two things by which he might stand in the presence of the Judge, not in fear of trial, but before a loving Creator of His believers.

13.20.0.en: This is what drives him to long to stand before God, and not to wish to hide from His presence as our first parents did when they thought that the shade of the fig tree would hide them from their Creator. But what are these two things? He pointed to them in the following phrase [21].

13.20.1.en: * God Himself says through the prophet: "I am the God who is near, and not the God who is far off" (Jer 23:23) LXX.

13.20.2.en: Fr. Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrrhus * Wherever you are, God comes to you if He finds chambers in your soul in which He can dwell.

13.20.3.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa * The Holy Trinity is near to all things, but not all things are near to Him.

13.20.4.en: The so-called Dionysius the Areopagite * Let the living God be present always in your mind. For your mind itself is in His likeness, also invisible and incomprehensible, and not represented in any form, and yet by its will the whole body is moved.

13.20.5.en: St. Melito, Bishop of Sardis Withdraw thine hand far from me: and let not thy dread make me afraid [21].

13.20.6.en: Perhaps by the two things he meant the following: 1. "Withdraw thine hand far from me": perhaps he asked Him not to remove the trial from him, but to lighten it. In lightening it he finds his opportunity for calm and freedom from distress, so that he may be free to speak with God. He does not ask for relief of his pains to boast before his friends that he is not wicked as they claimed, for what concerns him is to stand in the presence of God. 2. Job knows the awe of God; this awe is a source of joy and delight to the faithful believer, and not a source of terror!

13.20.7.en: * [I need two things, and then I will not hide myself from thy face] [20]. What are the two things that Job needs from God; these two which, he says, if he obtains them he will not hide himself from the face of the Judge?

13.20.8.en: [Hold back thine hand from me, and let not thy fear terrify me] [21]... Of this David said: [Remove thy strokes from me; I am wasted by the might of thine hand] (Ps 39:10)... You are incorruptible, but I am corruptible (Rom 1:23). You are the Lord, and I am a servant, like a wrestler in training, like an armed soldier. You speak, and I answer; not in boldness do I oppose, but out of desire to obtain wisdom, and to learn through speaking and listening.

13.20.9.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem Pope Gregory (the Great) sees in these two requests, that He hold back His hand and not let His fear terrify him, a prophecy of the longing for the age of grace, in which the blows of divine wrath for breaking the Law do not befall believers, and in which believers no longer worship God through fear as in the Old Testament, but through love. [Righteousness cannot be perfected by fear, and according to the voice of John: [Perfect love casteth out fear] (1 Jn 4:18). And Paul offers rest to the children of adoption, saying: "For ye have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear; but ye have received the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father" (Rom 8:15). Therefore, in the voice of humanity longing for the removal of the severity of the stroke of the Law, and with a fervent desire to advance from fear to love, he specifies in prayer two things that God should remove from him, saying: [Withdraw thine hand far from me, and let not thy dread make me afraid]. Remove me from the severity of the stroke, lift the weight of terror; and when the grace of love shines upon me, pour upon me the spirit of assurance. If I am not removed from the rod and from the terror, I know that I shall not be withdrawn from the firmness of Your examination. He who serves You not on the basis of love but on the basis of fear cannot be justified before You.]

13.21.0.en: Then call thou, and I will answer: or let me speak, and answer thou me [22].

13.21.1.en: By these two things he is in the presence of God and enters into a delightful dialogue. God speaks and Job answers, and Job speaks and God answers. This is the mutual love between God and His believers. This is the wonderful boldness we have when we stand before the throne of divine grace.

13.21.2.en: * [Call me, and I will answer; or let me speak, and answer thou me]... God's call to us is His esteem of us in love and His choosing of us, and our answer is our submission in obedience to His love by good works... He who runs eagerly, longing for the eternal world, examines his works, sets himself to act with great precision, and examines himself thoroughly lest there be found in him anything by which he would oppose the face of his Creator.

13.22.s.en: 7. Why do You hide Your face from me?

13.22.0.en: 23 "How many are mine iniquities and sins? make me to know my transgression and my sin. 24 Wherefore hidest thou thy face, and holdest me for thine enemy? 25 Wilt thou frighten a driven leaf? and wilt thou pursue the dry stubble? 26 For thou writest bitter things against me, and makest me to possess the iniquities of my youth, 27 so that thou hast put my feet in the stocks, and lookest narrowly unto all my paths; thou hast dug upon the roots of my feet. 28 And I am like a thing that is consumed by decay, like a garment that is moth eaten."

13.22.1.en: How many are mine iniquities and sins?

13.22.2.en: Make me to know my transgression and my sin [23].

13.22.3.en: Now, standing in the presence of the Lord, Job asks God about his iniquities and sins, that He may reveal them to him, so that he may confess them and ask pardon for them in a spirit of humility, not fearing exposure before himself.

13.22.4.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) says that there is a difference between crimes and iniquities. Crimes are far heavier than the measure of sin, whereas iniquity does not exceed the weight of sin. When an offering is commanded according to the Law, it is without doubt imposed for "sin" and at the same time for "iniquity" also. A crime is not accomplished except by deed, while iniquity is usually committed in thought alone.

13.23.0.en: Wherefore hidest thou thy face, and holdest me for thine enemy? [24]

13.23.1.en: Job confesses that he is a sinner and iniquitous, but in a spirit of humility and repentance he asks his divine Savior not to hide His face from him, nor to count him an enemy; for with all his weaknesses and sins he will not cease to ask, that he may enjoy fellowship with God his Creator.

13.23.2.en: * [Why do You hide Your face, and count me Your enemy?] [24] Man enjoyed the light of inward contemplation in Paradise, but when he was pleased with himself he departed from himself. He lost the light of the Creator, and fled from His face to the trees of Paradise. After he had committed his sin, he feared to see Him whom he had formerly loved. But note that punishment was brought upon him after the sin, yet after the punishment he returned to love, for he found the results of his disobedience, and the Face which he feared while in sin, when he awoke to sound understanding, he began to seek anew through the punishment, in order to flee from the darkness of the state of blindness that had come upon him, and he drew back in terror from this solitude that kept him from seeing his Creator.

13.24.0.en: Wilt thou frighten a driven leaf? and wilt thou pursue the dry stubble! [25]

13.24.1.en: Job entreats God, making himself very small before God and before himself, so he counts himself like a dry leaf of a tree that flies in haste and falls to the ground, and dry stubble moved by the winds... He is trodden down by his corrupt nature, so is it fitting for God's dignity that he who is already trodden down should be trodden down? Or to crush a person who has no power to resist?

13.24.2.en: "Thou carriest them away as with a flood; they are as a sleep: in the morning they are like grass which passeth away" (Ps 90:5).

13.24.3.en: "When the wicked spring as the grass, and when all the workers of iniquity do flourish; it is that they shall be destroyed for ever" (Ps 92:7).

13.24.4.en: "My days are like a shadow that declineth; and I am withered like grass" (Ps 102:11).

13.24.5.en: "As for man, his days are as grass: as a flower of the field, so he flourisheth" (Ps 103:15).

13.24.6.en: "Let them be as the grass upon the housetops, which withereth afore it groweth up" (Ps 129:6).

13.24.7.en: "Therefore their inhabitants were of small power, they were dismayed and confounded: they were as the grass of the field, and as the green herb, as the grass on the housetops, and as corn blasted before it be grown up" (Isa 37:27).

13.24.8.en: "For the sun is no sooner risen with a burning heat, but it withereth the grass, and the flower thereof falleth, and the grace of the fashion of it perisheth: so also shall the rich man fade away in his ways" (Jas 1:11).

13.24.9.en: "For all flesh is as grass, and all the glory of man as the flower of grass. The grass withereth, and the flower thereof falleth away" (1 Pet 1:24).

13.24.10.en: * [Has Your authority been shown over a leaf of a tree driven here and there? And will You follow the track of dry stubble (the remains of the harvest)?] [25]

13.24.11.en: What is man but a leaf that fell from the tree in Paradise?

13.24.12.en: What is he with whom the wind of temptation plays, whom the storms of his passions lift up, but a leaf of a tree?

13.24.13.en: The mind of man is stirred by many storms when he suffers temptations. So he is often stirred by anger. And when anger passes, empty merriment follows. He is drawn off by the goad of lust, lifted up by pride, and sometimes plunged by increasing fear to what is under the dust. Thus when a man sees himself raised and carried by many such storms of temptation, he becomes like a leaf of a tree. Therefore it was well said by Isaiah the prophet: [We all do fade as a leaf; and our iniquities, like the wind, have taken us away] (cf. Isa 64:6).

13.24.14.en: * We see that what we say passes away, while what we write remains; therefore it is said of God not only that He speaks but that He writes bitter things, since His blows upon us remain for a long time. Once it was said to the man who sinned: [Dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return] (c), and angels appeared many times and gave commandments to men. And Moses, the receiver of the Law, defined sins by firm means. And the Son of the Father, the Most High and Only-Begotten, came to save us. He swallowed up death by His death. He declared that He had shown eternal life for us in Himself. Yet this sentence that was passed in Paradise concerning the death of our body has remained unchanged from the beginning of the human race to the end of the world. For "What man is he that liveth, and shall not see death?" (Ps 89:48), and also: [Thou, even thou, art to be feared: and who may stand in thy sight when once thou art angry?] (Ps 76:7). For having been angry once when man sinned in Paradise, He established the sentence of death for our body.

13.24.16.en: * [Their years are as things of no value; in the morning they are like grass which passeth away] (Ps 90:5).. Such are these things which did not exist before their coming, and when they come to be here they soon pass away, for they come here only to pass... They come to fall into death, and dry up in a carcass, and wither in the dust. What is this but the body in which are the hateful fleshly lusts?

13.24.17.en: * Those who do not think uprightly in their hearts look upon the wicked when they are like green grass, that is, when they are prospering for a time. Why do they look upon them? "That they shall be destroyed for ever." They look to their temporary prosperity and imitate them, and wish to prosper with them for a time, and perish with them for ever.

13.24.18.en: * While you say that in this age everything passes away like a shadow, you do not pass away like a shadow. "My days pass away like a shadow, and I am withered like grass".. But the grass, when it is moistened with the Savior's blood, flourishes again. I have become dry like grass; for as a man I have suffered from Your just judgment, because "Thou shalt arise, and have mercy upon Zion: for the time to favour her, yea, the set time, is come" (Ps 102:13).

13.24.19.en: * "As for man, his days are as grass" (Ps 103:15). Let man realize what he is; let no man boast. "His days are as grass." Why should the grass boast, which flourishes now and in a short time withers? Why should the grass boast, which blooms only for a brief period, until the sun grows hot? It is therefore good for us that His mercy come upon us, and make gold of the grass! [As a flower of the field, so he flourisheth] (d). All the loftiness of the human race, honors and powers and wealth and pride and threats, is the flower of grass. That house flourishes, and this family is great, and that family grows; how many flourish, and how many years do they live! To you they are many years, but to God it is a short time; God's reckonings are not like yours. Compared with the length of life through long ages, the flower of any house is like the flower of grass. Hardly does the beauty of the year last throughout the whole year. Everything that flourishes, everything that is filled with the warmth of heat, everything that is beautiful will not last, indeed will not remain even a full year...! He has sent us His Word, His Word who abides for ever... Do not marvel that you will share His eternity, for He shared your grass. Will He who took from you what is lowly begrudge giving you what is exalted?

13.25.0.en: St. Augustine For thou writest bitter things against me, and makest me to possess the iniquities of my youth [26].

13.26.0.en: In his talks with his friends, when he compares himself with mankind, he affirms that he is righteous and not wicked as his friends claim. And when he speaks with the Holy One he confesses the iniquities of his youth, and asks Him to explain to him why He leaves him to be consumed as by decay, or like a garment that the moth eats [28]!

13.26.1.en: He says to God: If You record my sins and falls, they are bitter, and I will not justify myself from them; and if You record my iniquities, they are the iniquities of my youth. I know them well and do not deny them, but I remember Your love, O Forgiver of sins and iniquities.

13.26.2.en: The prophet David asks the Teacher not to remember his sins but to remember him as His beloved creature, who has his own particular value, not through any merit of his own, but for the sake of God's mercies and goodness, and for His holy name. He says: "Remember not the sins of my youth, nor my transgressions: according to thy mercy remember thou me for thy goodness' sake, O LORD" (Ps 25:7). The thief on the right asked the true Teacher to remember him when He came into His kingdom, and He did not remember his crimes nor his sins, but carried him to Paradise, justified in the merits of the precious Blood. So when we ask the Lord to remember us, He answers, saying: "I, even I, am he that blotteth out thy transgressions for mine own sake, and will not remember thy sins" (Isa 43:25). St. Paul commands his disciple Timothy: "Flee also youthful lusts: but follow righteousness, faith, charity, peace, with them that call on the Lord out of a pure heart" (2 Tim 2:22).

13.26.3.en: * "Why hast thou written evil things against me, and chargest me with the sins of my youth?" (Job 13:26) LXX.

13.26.4.en: He truly and fittingly makes this period of life (youth) the cause of his complaint, because in general in this period a person is unsteady with regard to sin.

13.26.5.en: Truly childhood is marked by innocence, and old age by wisdom. And early manhood, which adjoins the stage of youth, is regarded as the stage of gaining a good reputation, and the person feels ashamed if he commits a sin. But the stage of youth alone bears the mark of weakness and feeble counsel, with zeal in sin, and contempt for those who offer them counsel, while they are prepared to be deceived by pleasures. For the same reason David wonderfully asked pardon from the Lord for all that he fell into in that period, when he said: [Remember not the sins of my youth, nor my ignorance] (Ps 25:7). For in that period the majority suffer from the inflammation of lusts and their burning with the heat of hot blood.

13.26.6.en: St. Ambrose * [Why do You write my evils against me? and charge me with the sins of my youth?] Concerning the writing, He said: "Cursed is the ground for thy sake; in sorrow shalt thou eat of it all the days of thy life; thorns also and thistles shall it bring forth to thee; and thou shalt eat the herb of the field; in the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread, till thou return unto the ground; for out of it wast thou taken: for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return" (Gen 3:17-19). All mankind was condemned by all these, as though for a good reason these lines were written concerning the righteous and the wicked. In the same way God lays upon each one the sins of Adam's youth, for Adam was still young when he tasted the harmful food. This is the reason that not only he, but we also, his offspring, are prevented from gathering from the tree of life (Gen 3:22-24) which is in Paradise.

13.26.7.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * [Remember not the sins of my youth, nor my ignorance] (Ps 25:7). My transgressions and my impudent boldness and my ignorance, do not keep them for vengeance, but forget them. "According to thy mercy remember thou me" (Ps 25:7). Truly remember me not according to the wrath that I deserve, but according to Your mercy that befits You... not according to my merits but according to Your goodness, O Lord.

13.26.8.en: St. Augustine so that thou hast put my feet in the stocks, and lookest narrowly unto all my paths; thou hast dug upon the roots of my feet [27].

13.26.9.en: I have been disciplined because of my weaknesses and the iniquities of my youth; I have become like a prisoner whose feet are put in the stocks, unable to move. I will not flee from the blows of Your discipline.

13.26.10.en: You know all my paths, and You discipline me even for my hidden thoughts or my wayward glances. You record on the soles of my feet all that I have committed, and I do not deny what I have done.

13.26.11.en: * [Thou hast put my feet in the stocks], because our feet have been prevented from walking to enjoy the benefits of Paradise. For God [looks narrowly at our works]. Concerning the disobedience of the commandment that Adam committed, God condemned the whole human race which is his offspring. In any case, since He is a doer of good and a lover of man (Wis 7:23), He [looks narrowly at our works]. If they are evil, we ascribe them to ourselves, as being in the likeness of the old Adam, and we fall under the discipline that came upon him. But if they are good works, we shall be saved from the curse, and set free from the penalties (2 Cor 11:4), in the likeness of the new Adam, and through Him we receive the annulment of our great distress.

13.26.12.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * [Thou hast put my feet in the stocks]... This means: You have bound them. [You have dug upon the roots of my feet (my heels)] meaning that You attacked me wholly, and searched me to the depths; You struck my feet and my head, and left no part of me sound. Again, he speaks of the seriousness of his trial; he mocks the lowliness of nature.

13.26.13.en: St. John Chrysostom * God put man's foot in the stocks, in order to bind his evil entirely by a strong, firm judgment.

13.26.14.en: * [And thou lookest narrowly unto all my paths, thou settest a print upon the heels of my feet] [27]... The prints of the feet may be the many things that are done wrongly, for they perceive... Usually when we do wrong things and our brothers see them, we are a bad example to them, and our feet have turned aside from the way, and we leave all our crooked footprints to those who follow us, so that by our conduct we have led the consciences of others to stumbling.

13.26.15.en: But all these things Almighty God examines with precision, and weighs each of them in judgment. But when can man, bound as he is by the weakness of the flesh, have the power to stand against all these precisely and keep the straight line of the thought of the heart without moving? Therefore he says: [Who am I? As a rotten thing that consumeth, as a garment that is moth eaten] [28]... For man is like a rotten thing that perishes, for the corruption of his body scatters him. And because the temptation of uncleanness springs up in him from no other source than himself, like the moth, so temptation destroys the body, as the moth spoils the garment from what comes out of it; for man contains in himself the opportunity from which temptation comes forth, therefore the moth spoils the garment, while the moth comes forth from the garment itself.

13.26.17.en: And I am like a thing that is consumed by decay, like a garment that is moth eaten [28].

13.26.18.en: Job confesses that he goes from corruption to corruption because of his sins, as though the worm had worn out his bones and the moth had eaten his garment (his body); his depths are corrupted by the worm of sin and his body worn out by the moth of iniquity... But there is One who rescues the soul from corruption, and gives the body eternal glory when the corruptible puts on incorruption, and the spiritual body takes the place of the earthly.

13.26.19.en: * If you wish, you can be a slave to the passions. And if you wish, you can be freed from them and not submit to their yoke, for God created you and gave you this authority.

13.26.20.en: He who overcomes the passions of the flesh is crowned with incorruption. For if there were no passions, there could be no virtues, and consequently God would not give crowns to those who deserve them.

13.26.21.en: * He who understands what the body is, that it is corruptible and short-lived, understands also that the soul is heavenly and immortal, that it is a breath from God, and is joined to the body until it advances and rises toward likeness to God.

13.26.23.en: I fall into Your hand, O my God,
